headline: AI could increase R-star and sustain higher equilibrium interest rates even as it lowers inflation, challenging the consensus that AI productivity leads to rate cuts

However, she argues that AI can simultaneously lower inflation and raise interest rates by increasing potential growth and therefore raising R* (the neutral rate of interest). Because AI generates such strong demand for investment and capital, the economy may need to operate at a higher equilibrium rate. She also raises the fiscal angle: if AI profits accrue predominantly to capital rather than labour, tax revenues may disappoint since labour income is taxed at higher rates than capital, potentially sustaining deficits and term premium.
quote: I was thinking of a very interesting paradox because we think long run, at least everybody seems to agree that AI is going to lower inflation. Therefore, the Fed can cut interest rates. And interest rates have to be lower. But I think what people miss is that you can have lower inflation and higher interest rates because of the implications of AI on R*. So AI can increase potential growth, which can increase R*, and essentially means the economy needs, because there is so much demand for investment and capital, the economy needs to run at a higher equilibrium interest rate. So I feel like everything is pointing toward this world with higher interest rates for longer.

reasoning: Rowan argues that the Industrial Revolution legacy of passive learning is no longer fit for purpose. AI can personalise education to the individual, automate grading and discipline, and free teachers to act as creative synthesisers. The value proposition of expensive traditional universities is undermined when the world's best teaching can be personalised and delivered at scale.
quote: Why should university be so expensive when the world's best teachers are available to all of us and their knowledge can be parceled up and personalized for delivery to what you or your child needs at that time?
episode_title: Humans vs. Machines: David Rowan on Curiosity, Creativity, and the Future of AI

headline: US EV policy reversal materially narrows the addressable market for pure electric vehicles, shifting demand toward E-REV and hybrid powertrains
reasoning: The US government eliminated consumer subsidies for pure EV adoption and relaxed tailpipe emissions standards, leaving the US pure EV market dependent solely on customers whose duty cycles suit short-range commuting. This policy shift, combined with persistently high battery costs, means the mass-market EV opportunity in the US is substantially smaller than previously assumed. Ford's strategy now centres on E-REV and hybrid solutions for towing and work-use customers.
quote: Electrification in the US, especially after the policy change, is really going to be left with the customers who actually drive a duty cycle that makes sense for pure electric, which is basically people who drive their vehicles for commuting short distances.
episode_title: The Long View: Jim Farley, President and CEO, Ford

headline: BYD and Chinese OEMs cited as structurally superior EV engineers with best-in-class cost structure and global expansion ambitions
reasoning: After tearing down BYD and Tesla vehicles, Ford's engineering team concluded that Chinese OEMs engineer the entire vehicle around the battery budget, spending more on ancillary systems to shrink battery size, unlike Ford's ICE-prejudiced approach. Farley believes some Chinese OEMs will become top-five global automakers, are already the largest exporters of automobiles globally, and are beginning to localise production in Europe and Southeast Asia.
quote: I have no doubt some of them will be the top five globally, like Toyota and Volkswagen have been. And they're now not only exporting in huge volume, they're now starting to localize production in Europe and Southeast Asia.
episode_title: The Long View: Jim Farley, President and CEO, Ford

headline: China automotive market dominated by local brands with 50% excess capacity, making China the world's largest auto exporter and a growing competitive threat globally
reasoning: China accounts for roughly one-third of all global vehicle sales and its OEM capacity is approximately 50% higher than its domestic market. Western brands have lost dominance in China to local players such as BYD, NIO, XPeng and GEELY. Chinese OEMs are now aggressively localising production in Europe and Southeast Asia, and in markets like Australia have grown from 10% to 20% market share with a trajectory toward 50%.
quote: The market is 29 million. Approximately a third of all vehicles sold on this planet are sold in China. And the capacity is 50% higher than their local market. So they're the largest exporter of automobiles.
episode_title: The Long View: Jim Farley, President and CEO, Ford

headline: Ford CEO Farley pivots away from pure EV investment, cancels next-gen Lightning and SUV lineup in favour of E-REV and hybrid strategy
reasoning: Ford cancelled its next-generation all-electric Lightning and planned SUV lineup after concluding battery costs would not fall to levels where customers would pay the required prices. The company is instead focusing on its Skunk Works UEV platform (built with no ICE prejudice), E-REV technology, and hybridisation of its existing lineup. Farley noted investors had already modelled this outcome and the announcement was received positively by the market.
quote: We had a great next-generation all-electric Lightning and lots of SUEs planned that our competitors had just come out with. We canceled all of that. We stopped it all.
episode_title: The Long View: Jim Farley, President and CEO, Ford

headline: T-Mobile CEO warns AI disruption is broader and deeper than currently appreciated, with financial services already getting a taste
reasoning: The CEO argues that AI will disrupt multiple industries in ways that are not yet fully understood, noting financial services had already experienced a preview. He believes the only response is to simultaneously plan for being disrupted while actively seeking to be the disruptor, and expects the landscape to look materially different within three years.
quote: I think all sorts of industries will be disrupted... And I think we shouldn't shy away from the fact that we could be disrupted as well. I think we're, I don't think we're even scratched the surface of the disruptive part of the technology.
episode_title: The Long View: Srini Gopalan, CEO, T-Mobile

headline: T. Rowe Price host highlights T-Mobile's dramatic subscriber growth and counter-positioning strategy as a textbook investment case
